newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Swiss see bleak economic performance in 1996.
newsitem.headline: Swiss see bleak economic performance in 1996.

text.p: A report on Tuesday that the Swiss gross domestic product remained stubbornly in negative territory added yet another piece of bad news to what is turning out to be a memorably bad year for the Swiss.

The Swiss Federal Statistics Office said Switzerland's Gross Domestic Product (GDP) fell at an annual, seasonally-adjusted rate of 0.9 percent in the second quarter of 1996 compared with the first quarter. It was the sixth quarterly decline in a row.
The news added to evidence that no economic revival is likely to happen this year.

"Switzerland is in a recession, and it is a recession which followed a weak revival. The general sentiment has to be "dull' after five years of no income growth in Switzerland," said Klaus Wellershoff, head of Swiss macro economic research for SBC Warburg.

The country is suffering from a slew of other problems, ranging from bad press related to recent reports citing Switzerland as a haven for Nazi assets in World War II, to a proposal by the Swiss cabinet on Monday that the country should slaughter up to 230,000 cows to eliminate mad cow disease in the country.

Even Swiss cheese, a staple export product, has been cast in a bad light by a recent scandal involving the half state-owned Swiss Cheese Union, which was found to have undercut European cheese export prices in a kickback scheme.

"These things aggravate the underlying problem, and that is that since 1991 we have had practically no growth," said Willie Roth, spokesman for the KOF Institute at the Zurich Federal Technical College. The KOF publishes a monthly business barometer.

"Switzerland must come out of this stagnation. The only possibility seems to be for exports to improve and then, sometime in future, income will increase. As long as that doesn't happen, I don't see how domestic demand is going to improve," said Roth.
The KOF now forecasts GDP at minus 0.2 percent, but that forecast is likely to be revised down on October 2, Roth said.
Growth forecasts for 1997 could be revised down as well.
Swiss economists note that Swiss unemployment, while low at only 4.5 percent, is still high in historical terms, and adds to worries when wage growth is at a virtual standstill.
The problem has been aggravated by a slowdown in the service sector, which comprises 68 percent of total GDP, according to the Swiss Federal Statistics Office.
Bruno Parnisari, economist at Federal Statistics Office said that in future, services are likely to be even more more important in terms of the economy.

Martin Jetzer, chief economist at Guyerzeller Bank, said the importance of the service industry had made the entire economy more volatile. He noted that tourism, which is experiencing negative growth, alone accounts for seven percent of the GDP.

Consolidation in major Swiss companies announced this year, including a planned merger between pharmaceutical firms Ciba-Geigy AG and Sandoz AG, and restructuring in the banking industry, also have caused worries about jobs.

"Senior executives who 10 years ago would have predicted steady income growth, are saying today they are sure they won't earn more, and could earn less in three years. In worst case, they could be on street," Jetzer said.
Many economists lay blame for Switzerland's weak economy on the strong Swiss franc, which curbs exports.
The Federal Statistics office noted that exports in the second quarter fell for the first time in three years. The situation was similar for imports.

The franc has been pushed higher by safe-haven demand tied to uncertainty about European Monetary Union (EMU). Switzerland declined to join EMU, which foresees phasing in a single currency among members starting in 1999.
But Jack Tatom, international economist at Union Bank of Switzerland, said that another major problem has been weakness in export countries like Germany, Italy and France.
"These are the big export markets. I really think it is the weakness in demand in foreign countries. UBS is forecasting negative growth for Switzerland of 0.6 percent in 1996.
